title: Active Directory Trusts: How Cross-Domain and Cross-Forest Movement Is Detected and Contained
intro: An Active Directory trust is a configured relationship that lets domain controllers in one domain accept and vouch for the identities of another domain or forest. This lesson explains how trusts work, how an attacker who owns one domain uses them to reach a neighbor, and which telemetry and controls let you detect and contain that movement.

sections.heading: Domains, trees, forests, and what a trust actually is
sections.content:
An Active Directory **domain** is an administrative and replication unit. It has its own directory partition, its own domain controllers (DCs), its own krbtgt account, and its own SID prefix (S-1-5-21 followed by three 32-bit numbers). A **tree** is a set of domains that share a contiguous DNS namespace, for example corp.example.com and emea.corp.example.com. A **forest** is one or more trees that share a single schema, a single Configuration partition, and a global catalog. A **trust** is a relationship between two domains that allows a DC in one domain to accept an authentication performed by a DC in the other, so a user from one side can be granted access to resources on the other side.

A useful analogy is two countries that recognize each other's passports. The border officer (the trusting DC) does not know the traveler personally; it checks that the passport (the ticket) was issued by an authority it has agreed to believe, and then it reads the stamps on the passport (the group SIDs) to decide what the traveler may do. If the issuing authority is corrupt, every passport it prints is believed. That is the entire risk model of trusts: **the trusting side delegates its judgment about identity to the trusted side.**

**The forest, not the domain, is the security boundary.** This surprises many analysts. Inside a forest, every DC replicates the Configuration and Schema partitions, intra-forest trusts honor the SIDs placed in tickets by any domain's KDC, and a Domain Admin of a child domain controls the DCs that mint those tickets. Microsoft's own guidance is that you cannot rely on domain boundaries to contain a determined, privileged attacker inside a forest. If one domain in a forest is fully compromised, assume the forest root is reachable.

**What a trust looks like as data.** Each trust is stored as a trustedDomain object (TDO) in the System container of the domain partition. Important attributes:

- trustPartner and flatName: the DNS and NetBIOS names of the other side.
- trustDirection: 1 inbound, 2 outbound, 3 bidirectional.
- trustType and trustAttributes: bit flags that encode transitivity, forest trust, selective authentication, and SID filtering state.
- securityIdentifier: the domain SID of the other side, which the filter uses later.

The trust also has a trust account and a shared secret called the inter-realm trust key, stored in the TDO and rotated automatically by default about every 30 days. That secret is what the two KDCs use to protect referral tickets, which makes it a high-value credential.

**What an analyst should ask.** Which trusts exist, in which direction, who administers the other side, and what has been granted to foreign principals on our side? A trust inventory is a detection prerequisite: you cannot call a cross-realm ticket anomalous if you never learned which realms are expected to talk to each other.

The attack techniques that forge tickets, such as Golden Ticket forgery and DCSync, are covered in their own lessons on Kerberos ticket forgery and directory replication abuse; here we focus on what changes when a trust boundary is involved.

sections.heading: Trust types, direction, and transitivity
sections.content:
Six trust types appear in practice. The table summarizes the properties that matter to a defender.

| Trust type | How it is created | Direction | Transitive | SID filtering | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parent-child | Automatic when a child domain is created | Two-way | Yes | Not applied (same forest) | Hierarchy inside a tree |
| Tree-root | Automatic when a new tree joins a forest | Two-way | Yes | Not applied (same forest) | Links trees in one forest |
| Shortcut | Manual | One-way or two-way | Yes | Not applied (same forest) | Shortens the referral path between distant domains |
| External | Manual | One-way or two-way | No | Enabled by default (quarantine) | One domain in another forest or a legacy domain |
| Forest | Manual | One-way or two-way | Between all domains of both forests, not onward to a third forest | Enabled by default | Mergers, partner forests, resource forests |
| Realm | Manual | One-way or two-way | Configurable | Not applicable (non-Windows Kerberos) | MIT or other Kerberos realms |

**Direction is the part people invert.** In a one-way trust where domain A trusts domain B, A is the **trusting** domain and B is the **trusted** domain. Users in B can be authorized to resources in A. The trust arrow in diagrams points from the trusting domain to the trusted domain, while access flows the opposite way. For a defender the useful rule is this: **the domain whose compromise matters is the trusted one**, because its identities are believed by the trusting side. A resource forest that trusts an acquired company's forest is exposed to that company's weakest domain.

**Transitivity** means that if A trusts B and B trusts C, then A trusts C automatically. Parent-child and tree-root trusts are transitive, which is why every domain in a forest implicitly trusts every other. Forest trusts are transitive across the two forests' domains but do not chain onward: if forest 1 trusts forest 2 and forest 2 trusts forest 3, forest 1 does not trust forest 3. External trusts are non-transitive and name exactly one domain. This matters when scoping an incident: a transitive path gives an attacker more doors, and a non-transitive external trust limits blast radius to a single domain pair.

**Within the forest versus across it.** The trustAttributes flags separate the cases. A within-forest trust (flag 0x20) is not SID-filtered. A forest-transitive trust (0x8) is filtered by default. A quarantined external trust (0x4) has SID filtering on. A cross-organization trust (0x10) has selective authentication enabled. Reading these four bits on every TDO is a fast, high-value audit that takes minutes.

**Shortcut trusts** deserve a special note. They are created by administrators to speed up authentication in large forests, they add a new path and a new trust key to protect, and they are frequently forgotten. Every extra trust is an extra shared secret and an extra place for tickets to cross.

**Mental model for triage.** When you see a cross-domain event, classify it first: same forest or different forest, direction, transitive path used, and whether filtering applies. Those four answers tell you what an attacker could have forged and what the control should have stripped.

sections.heading: How authentication crosses a trust: referrals, inter-realm TGTs, and SIDs
sections.content:
Suppose a user in domain ACQ (the trusted domain) opens a file share on a server in domain CORP (the trusting domain). Conceptually the Kerberos exchange looks like this:

1. The user logs on to a DC in ACQ and receives a normal TGT (event 4768 on the ACQ DC).
2. The client asks its own KDC for a service ticket for the CORP server. The ACQ KDC does not hold that service account, but it knows a trust to CORP exists.
3. The ACQ KDC returns a **referral**: an **inter-realm TGT**, a ticket-granting ticket for the krbtgt service of CORP, encrypted with the **inter-realm trust key** shared between the two domains. On the ACQ DC this shows up as a 4769 with a service name that looks like krbtgt/CORP rather than a normal host or cifs SPN.
4. The client presents the referral to a CORP DC. That DC decrypts it with the same trust key, which proves the ACQ KDC issued it, and then issues the actual service ticket (another 4769, this time on the CORP DC, with a foreign account domain).
5. The client presents the service ticket to the file server, which builds a logon session (event 4624, logon type 3) for an account whose domain is ACQ.

In a forest with several domains, step 3 can chain: the client is referred up the tree toward the forest root and back down, or directly via a shortcut trust, and each hop is a separate inter-realm TGT and a separate 4769.

**Where authorization data rides: the PAC.** Kerberos only proves who you are. What you may do comes from the **Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC)** that the user's home KDC places inside the ticket. The PAC lists the user SID, primary group, and group SIDs from the home domain, plus an **ExtraSids** list. ExtraSids carries, among other things, the values from the account's **sIDHistory** attribute, which was designed for domain migrations so that a migrated user keeps access granted to the old SID. The resource-side DC copies those SIDs into the access token it builds. So a SID that appears in the PAC is treated as a real group membership.

**What the trusting KDC verifies and what it cannot.** The trusting DC can verify the trust-key signature, which proves the ticket came from the partner KDC. It cannot independently verify the truth of the group list; it must believe the partner. That is exactly why the partner's honesty is the security assumption, and why a control is needed on the receiving side that rejects SIDs the partner has no business asserting.

**The control point: SID filtering.** When a ticket arrives over a filtered trust, the trusting DC compares each SID in the PAC against the domain SID recorded in the TDO (and the domain SIDs listed in the forest trust information). SIDs that do not belong to the trusted side, or that fall in the privileged built-in range, are removed before the token is built, and an event 4675 can be logged. Within a forest this filtering is not applied to the same degree, which is the core reason a child domain can reach its parent.

**Other relevant behavior.** Since the security updates of 2019, TGT delegation across forest trusts is disabled by default, so unconstrained-delegation hosts in the trusting forest cannot capture TGTs of users from the other forest unless an admin explicitly enables it. Verify this setting rather than assuming it.

sections.heading: Trust discovery (T1482): normal versus suspicious enumeration
sections.content:
MITRE ATT&CK T1482, **Domain Trust Discovery**, is the Discovery technique an adversary uses to learn which domains trust each other and in which direction. The goal is planning: which neighbor can I reach, what does it trust, and where do privileged foreign principals live. Enumeration is cheap and quiet, so it is usually one of the first actions after the initial foothold on a domain-joined machine.

**How trusts are enumerated (what generates the telemetry):**

- **LDAP queries** for objects of class trustedDomain under the System container, or for the trustAttributes and trustDirection attributes. The query is a normal LDAP search that any authenticated user can run.
- **Netlogon RPC** calls that return the domain trust list, which is what the built-in nltest utility and the .NET and Win32 domain APIs use.
- **PowerShell** Active Directory cmdlets such as Get-ADTrust and Get-ADForest, which are LDAP and Active Directory Web Services (ADWS) under the hood.
- **Collectors** such as BloodHound ingestors, which pull trusts together with group and ACL data in one sweep.

Any authenticated domain user can read trust objects, so there is no access-denied signal and no failed-logon event. Detection therefore depends on **who** is asking, **from where**, and **what else** they did around it.

**What it looks like in the logs:**

| Source | Signal | What to inspect |
|---|---|---|
| Process creation (4688 with command line, Sysmon 1) | nltest with a domain_trusts or all_trusts switch, dsquery for trustedDomain, a PowerShell script block mentioning Get-ADTrust or GetAllTrustRelationships | Parent process, user, host role, time |
| PowerShell script block logging (4104) | .NET trust enumeration methods, collector modules | Script origin, encoded content |
| DC directory service diagnostics (event 1644, if enabled) | Expensive or inefficient LDAP searches containing objectClass=trustedDomain | Client IP, filter text, result count |
| Optional SACL on trustedDomain objects (4662) | Read-property access by an unexpected principal | Subject account, access mask |
| Defender for Identity | Directory-services and security-principal reconnaissance alerts | Source computer, queried object types |

**Normal versus suspicious.** Domain admins and migration teams run these commands during trust changes. Monitoring agents and some cloud sync products also read TDOs on a schedule. The baseline is: a small set of admin hosts, change windows, and named service accounts. Suspicious patterns:

- A workstation of a non-IT user, or a server with no AD role, enumerating trusts.
- Trust enumeration within minutes of a first-seen logon, an unusual process tree (a document handler spawning a shell), or alongside enumeration of privileged groups and SPNs.
- A burst that covers all trusts and all foreign security principals, typical of an automated collector.
- Enumeration on a host that later authenticates across the trust it just discovered.

**Analyst questions.** Is this host and account expected to do this? What happened on the host in the 30 minutes before? Did the same account authenticate to the foreign domain afterward? Discovery alone is low severity; discovery followed by cross-realm authentication from an account with no history of it is a pivot candidate and should be escalated.

sections.heading: The abuse, conceptually: why one owned domain threatens its neighbors
sections.content:
This section describes attacker intent so you can recognize it. It deliberately avoids tooling and procedure.

**Starting position.** The adversary has full control of one domain, typically through compromise of its krbtgt secret, a Domain Admin credential, or replicated directory secrets (see the DCSync and Golden Ticket lesson for how that is detected). Control of a domain means control of the KDC that vouches for that domain's users. The question the attacker now asks is: **what does a neighbor believe about me?**

**Intra-forest path (child to forest root).** Tickets minted by the child KDC carry a PAC. Because intra-forest trusts apply no SID filtering, the receiving parent DC accepts SIDs in the ExtraSids list. If an attacker who controls the child KDC's signing material places the SID of a highly privileged forest-root group (for example Enterprise Admins, whose SID ends in RID 519 under the root domain SID) into ExtraSids, the root domain treats the holder as a member. This is **SID-History injection** (ATT&CK T1134.005), here used in a forged-ticket form; the forged ticket itself is a Golden Ticket variant (T1558.001). The consequence is that child-domain compromise becomes forest-root compromise, which is the practical proof that the forest is the boundary.

**Cross-forest path.** Between forests the attacker's wish is the same: have the other forest's DCs believe privileged SIDs. Two raw ingredients are possible: the trust key (allowing a forged referral ticket) or the home domain's krbtgt. If SID filtering is **off or relaxed** (for example sIDHistory explicitly enabled on the trust for a long-finished migration), foreign privileged SIDs in the PAC are honored. If it is **on**, the trusting DC strips SIDs that do not belong to the trusted side, and the forgery yields little privilege. This is the heart of the defender's argument for filtering: the control converts a catastrophic assumption (the partner never lies) into a bounded one (the partner can only speak for itself).

**What filtering does not stop.** The attacker who owns the trusted domain can always act as any principal of the trusted domain, including the ones **legitimately granted** access on the trusting side. If a group from the trusted forest is a member of a local administrators group on servers in the trusting forest, compromise of the trusted forest reaches those servers with no forgery at all. SID filtering, selective authentication, and careful grants are complementary:

- Filtering limits what identities the partner can claim.
- Selective authentication limits which resources those identities can even request.
- Least-privilege grants limit what the permitted identities can do.

**Adjacent trust-related objectives to keep in mind:**

- Obtaining the **trust key** by replicating the trust account object, which looks like DCSync activity (T1003.006) targeting a trust account.
- Using **sIDHistory** as a persistence mechanism: adding a privileged SID to an ordinary account so that account is quietly privileged.
- Abusing **foreign security principals** and cross-domain group nesting that already exist.

**Why this matters for a SOC.** The attacker's value is in the PAC contents and the ticket path, neither of which are visible in a user-facing log. Your detections must therefore compare what the ticket claims against what the directory says is true, and against what history says is normal for that account and trust.

sections.heading: Detection: events and signals that expose cross-trust compromise
sections.content:
Collect security logs from **all DCs in all domains and forests you are responsible for** into one SIEM, with accurate time. Cross-realm detection fundamentally requires joining a ticket seen in one domain with the issuance seen in another.

| Signal | Event / source | What it indicates | Key fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| SIDs removed by the filter | 4675 (Audit Logon) on the trusting DC | A ticket from the trusted side carried SIDs it was not entitled to claim; high fidelity | Account, trust information, filtered SIDs |
| SID History added to an account | 4765 (success), 4766 (failure) | Migration tool or attacker adding sIDHistory; rare outside planned migrations | Target account, source SID, subject |
| Directory change to sIDHistory or TDO attributes | 5136 (DS Changes auditing) | Persistence or trust weakening | Attribute, old and new value |
| Trust created, removed, or modified | 4706, 4707, 4716; forest entries 4865, 4866, 4867 | Trust lifecycle change; should always map to a ticket | Domain name, trust direction, trust attributes |
| Service ticket with no preceding TGT | 4769 without a matching 4768 in the user's home domain | Forged-ticket pattern; classic Golden Ticket logic applied per realm | TargetUserName, TargetDomainName, IpAddress |
| Unexpected encryption or lifetime | 4769 TicketEncryptionType 0x17 where AES is the baseline | Downgrade or forged ticket; baseline first, because many trust keys are RC4 by default | TicketEncryptionType, TicketOptions |
| Foreign account with special privileges | 4624 logon type 3 plus 4672 and 4627 on a resource server | A foreign identity holding privileged group SIDs | Account domain, privilege list, group list |
| Replication of a trust account | 4662 with replication control GUIDs | Trust key theft | Properties, subject, source IP |
| Selective authentication denied | 4625 with status 0xC0000413 | An identity tried to reach a resource it was not explicitly allowed | Account, workstation, source IP |
| Defender for Identity | Forged-ticket and PAC anomaly alerts, DCSync, directory reconnaissance | Corroboration with ticket-level analysis | Alert evidence, source computer |

**How to read the key ones.**

Event **4675** is the strongest signal on a filtered trust. Legitimate users do not carry foreign privileged SIDs, so its appearance is rarely benign; the usual benign case is a stale sIDHistory from an old migration or a broken group-nesting configuration that you can identify by checking whether the SID is a real group.

The **4769 without 4768** logic needs cross-forest log availability. If an inter-realm service ticket arrives for user X from ACQ but ACQ's DCs never logged a 4768 for X in the preceding window (and no cached or renewed TGT explains it), the TGT was not issued by a real KDC exchange. Account for ticket renewal and TGT lifetime to avoid false positives.

**Nonexistent or mismatched identity.** Compare the user in the ticket against the directory: a user name that does not exist in the claimed domain, or a domain name with the wrong case or form, shows up in 4769 and 4624 fields and is a documented forged-ticket tell.

**What compromise looks like end to end:**

1. Discovery (T1482) on a host in the trusted domain.
2. Replication or secret extraction events on a DC.
3. A privileged-looking foreign account starting to authenticate to trusting-domain DCs and file servers at unusual hours.
4. 4672 special privileges and 4627 group lists that include SIDs with the trusting domain's privileged RIDs (512, 518, 519).
5. Follow-on movement: new services, scheduled tasks, or GPO changes in the trusting domain.

The **sequence** is the detection. Single events are noisy; the chain across two domains is not.

sections.heading: Defenses: SID filtering, selective authentication, and trust hygiene
sections.content:
Trust security is mostly configuration, which means it is mostly auditable. The table maps each control to what it prevents and how to verify it.

| Control | What it stops | How to verify | Caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| SID filtering (quarantine) on external and forest trusts | The partner asserting SIDs from outside its own domain, including privileged SIDs of the trusting forest | trustAttributes flags on each TDO (quarantine bit 0x4 on external trusts); the netdom trust quarantine query; absence of unexpected sIDHistory enablement | Not applied within a forest; disabling it for a migration must be time-boxed |
| Selective authentication | Foreign identities reaching servers they were not explicitly allowed to reach | Cross-organization bit 0x10 on the TDO; the Allowed to Authenticate permission on target computer objects | Operational overhead; needs a process for granting the permission |
| One-way trusts in the least-trust direction | Unneeded reverse exposure | trustDirection on both TDOs | Many trusts are created two-way by default and never revisited |
| Removing stale trusts | Forgotten paths and aging shared secrets | Inventory against business owner list; look for trusts to domains that no longer resolve | Confirm with the owner; removal breaks dependent access |
| Tiering and the enterprise access model | Privileged credentials landing on lower-trust systems | Review where Tier 0 accounts log on; check for foreign principals in Tier 0 groups | Needs identity and endpoint controls to be effective |
| Disabling TGT delegation across the trust | Captured TGTs of foreign users on delegation hosts | Setting on the trust and absence of unconstrained delegation on trust-facing servers | Verify, because the default moved over the years |
| Strong inter-realm key encryption | Offline cracking and downgrade of referral tickets | Trust encryption type, AES support flag | Some legacy realm trusts require RC4 |
| Audit policy and SACLs | Blind spots | 4675, 4765, 4706-4716 and 5136 present in the SIEM | Volume tuning on DCs |

**Design principles worth teaching your engineers:**

- **Trust only what is administered to your standard.** An acquired company's forest, a partner network, or a lab domain with weak credentials is a lower-trust domain. Treat the trust as if that forest is already hostile.
- **Prefer a resource-forest design with filtered, selectively authenticated forest trusts** over external trusts that were set up with default settings. Forest trusts apply modern filtering and support name-suffix routing exclusions.
- **Grant by group, audit the groups.** Foreign principals should appear in a small number of domain-local groups scoped to specific resources. Review the ForeignSecurityPrincipals container regularly.
- **Never leave sIDHistory enabled on a trust after a migration ends.** Clean sIDHistory from migrated accounts once the old SIDs are no longer referenced in ACLs.
- **Minimize privileged groups across a trust.** Domain Admins from one forest should not be members of local administrator groups in another.
- **Include trusts in change control.** Events 4706, 4707, 4716, and 4865-4867 should have a matching ticket, or they become an alert.

Microsoft has also moved away from recommending dedicated administrative forests for most organizations, in favor of the enterprise access model with privileged access workstations and separation of control, management, data, and user planes. The key lesson for the SOC is that a trust to an admin forest concentrates risk and needs the strictest monitoring.

**Detection engineering tie-in.** Convert each control into a monitor: alert when trustAttributes on any TDO changes, when sIDHistory is set on an account outside a migration window, and when 4675 occurs at all.

sections.heading: Incident response when a trust is abused
sections.content:
The first decision in the response is **scope**, and it is driven by the trust type, not by the evidence you have so far.

**Scope rules of thumb:**

- If the attacker reached **Domain Admin or equivalent in any domain of a forest**, treat the **entire forest** as compromised. Intra-forest trusts honor forged SIDs, so the attacker can be Enterprise Admin without ever logging on to the root.
- If a **filtered forest or external trust** was used, treat the trusted side as hostile and the trusting side as **exposed to the identities granted there**. Scope the trusting side by what foreign principals can reach, plus any evidence of 4675 or successful privileged access.
- If **SID filtering was disabled or sIDHistory enabled** on the trust, assume the filter did not protect you and widen the scope to everything the forged SIDs could access.

**Containment sequence (in practice):**

1. **Preserve evidence.** Collect DC security logs from both sides, memory and disk images from the pivot host, and the TDO attributes. Record trust attributes before changing anything.
2. **Cut the path, not the business, when possible.** Enable selective authentication with an empty allow list, tighten to a minimal set, or temporarily remove the trust if the business impact is acceptable. Removing a trust invalidates the shared secret path but also breaks legitimate access; coordinate with application owners.
3. **Enable or restore SID filtering** on the trust and remove any sIDHistory exception that is no longer required.
4. **Disable or reset accounts** that carry the suspicious SIDs, and remove unexpected sIDHistory values.
5. **Hunt for persistence** in both forests: new privileged accounts, GPO and scheduled task changes, AdminSDHolder modifications, and additional trust objects.

**Credential reset considerations.**

| Credential | Why it matters | Reset approach |
|---|---|---|
| krbtgt of every domain where the attacker had KDC-level access | Forged tickets signed with it remain valid until it is rotated | Reset twice per domain, with replication convergence and at least the maximum ticket lifetime between resets, in a controlled order |
| Inter-realm trust passwords | A forged referral using the trust key survives krbtgt resets | Reset the trust password on both sides (coordinate with the partner's administrators); verify the trust afterward |
| Privileged and service account secrets | Credentials seen in memory or replicated | Rotate with the tiering model, Tier 0 first |
| Directory service restore and other break-glass credentials | Used for persistence | Rotate and verify storage |

Two points are easy to miss. Resetting krbtgt **does not** invalidate tickets forged with a different secret, such as the trust key, and resetting the trust password **does not** invalidate tickets forged with the child krbtgt. Cover both. And a single krbtgt reset is insufficient because the previous password is retained for validation; the second reset removes it.

**Communication.** Cross-forest trusts imply a counterparty. Notify the partner organization through a defined contact, share indicators, and agree on timing for trust resets. In a merger or outsourcing, contracts often define security notification obligations that start here.

**Recovery and lessons.** After containment, decide whether to rebuild. When forest-level compromise is confirmed with high privilege, forest recovery or rebuild is the only way to be certain, and trust re-establishment should come last with filtering and selective authentication enabled from the first day.

sections.heading: Worked detection example: foreign tickets carrying unexpected privileged SIDs
sections.content:
**Scenario.** CORP (corp.example.com) is a resource forest. It has a forest trust with ACQ (acq.example.net), the forest of a recently acquired company with weaker administration. The trust is two-way, SID filtering is on (default), and selective authentication is off. Your SIEM collects security logs from DCs of both forests.

**The alert.** At 02:14 a rule on event 4675 fires on CORP-DC02. The relevant details:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Event | 4675, SIDs were filtered |
| Account | A user from the ACQ domain with a routine service-style name |
| Trust attributes | Forest transitive (0x8) |
| Filtered SIDs | Two SIDs under the CORP domain SID, with RIDs 512 and 519 |

This is the shape that matters: an identity from the trusted domain presented, in its PAC, privileged SIDs that belong to the **trusting** domain. A real KDC in ACQ has no reason to emit those.

**Step 1: Confirm it is real.** Compare the filtered SIDs against CORP's directory. RID 512 and 519 are Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins patterns of CORP. Check the account's sIDHistory in ACQ (if you have read access): if ACQ has a migration project from CORP that left stale SIDs, you may find a benign cause, but then the SIDs would be genuine old group SIDs rather than the top-privileged ones.

**Step 2: Check the ticket story.** Pull the 4769 on the CORP DC for the same account and client IP. Does the account have a matching 4768 on an ACQ DC in the last ten hours? Encryption type? If there is no TGT issuance in ACQ and the ticket lifetime or flags are unusual, a forged ticket is likely. Compare the client IP against ACQ's inventory.

**Step 3: Determine whether filtering held.** Look for 4624 type 3 logons by this account on CORP servers after the 4675, and for 4672 special privileges. If you see only filtered attempts and ordinary low-privileged access, the control worked. If you see privileged use, filtering was bypassed or a legitimately granted group is being abused, and the scope grows. Review the trust attributes now and compare to the last audit.

**Step 4: Scope the attacker's foothold.** The ticket implies the attacker holds ACQ krbtgt or the trust key. In ACQ look for DCSync-style 4662 events, process execution on DCs, and discovery (T1482) from the source IP in the days before. Search CORP for the same source IP and account across all servers.

**Step 5: Contain.**

- Turn on selective authentication on the trust with a minimal allow list; the attempts will now fail with status 0xC0000413.
- Block the source IP at the firewall and isolate the ACQ host if it is managed by you.
- Notify ACQ's administrators; begin the krbtgt double reset and trust password reset on both sides.
- Raise the incident severity to forest-level on the ACQ side.
- Search CORP for any foreign principal in privileged groups and for sIDHistory changes.

**Step 6: Learn.** Document that the control produced the signal. Add a standing detection for any 4675 on the trust, a monitor for trustAttributes changes, and a review of foreign group grants.

**What this teaches.** The attacker's intent was visible only because the control logged what it removed. Without SID filtering, the same ticket would have produced a normal-looking privileged logon.

quiz.question: An attacker has gained Domain Admin in a child domain of your forest. Which statement best reflects how you should scope the incident?

options.label: Treat the entire forest as compromised, because intra-forest trusts accept SIDs placed in tickets by the child KDC and the forest is the real boundary.
Treat only the child domain as compromised, because Domain Admin rights are scoped to the domain in which they were granted.
Treat the parent as exposed only if SID filtering was disabled on the parent-child trust, because filtering protects intra-forest paths.
Treat the forest as safe until the Enterprise Admins group shows a membership change recorded in a directory change event.

quiz.explanation: Intra-forest trusts (parent-child, tree-root, shortcut) do not apply SID filtering the way external and forest trusts do, so a party that controls a child KDC can place privileged forest-root SIDs into tickets and the parent honors them. That makes the forest, not the domain, the security boundary. The idea that Domain Admin is domain-scoped describes the intended design, not what an attacker with KDC-level control can achieve. Filtering is not the control that protects intra-forest paths, so waiting on a filtering setting is a mistake. Waiting for a group membership change is wrong because forged SIDs in a ticket grant privilege without any directory change.

quiz.question: A DC in your resource forest logs event 4675 for an account from a trusted forest, listing filtered SIDs with RIDs 512 and 519 under your own domain SID. What is the most accurate interpretation and next step?

options.label: The trusted forest's migration tool is working normally; close the event and document it as expected sIDHistory traffic.
The filter works as designed, but a trusted-side ticket claimed your privileged groups, so investigate forged tickets and trust-key exposure.
The trust is misconfigured and should be rebuilt immediately, since filtering events only occur when a trust is broken.
The user was added to Domain Admins in your domain, so review your own directory change events for the account.

quiz.explanation: Event 4675 records that SID filtering removed SIDs the trusted side was not entitled to assert. Privileged RIDs belonging to your own domain appearing in a foreign ticket are not an expected migration artifact, so the control is working and is simultaneously telling you the partner side may be compromised, which calls for ticket-level and trust-key investigation. Closing it as migration traffic ignores that the SIDs are top-privileged ones. The event does not indicate a broken trust; it shows filtering functioning. A foreign ticket claiming your groups does not mean your own directory was changed, so the change-event review is the wrong first step.

quiz.question: After confirming a forged-ticket attack through a trust, a team resets the krbtgt password twice in the compromised domain and declares the credential risk closed. What did they miss?

options.label: The krbtgt reset should happen only once, because a second reset breaks replication between domain controllers.
Only the forest root krbtgt matters, so resets in the child domains are unnecessary for a cross-trust incident.
The inter-realm trust password, because a ticket forged with the trust key stays valid after krbtgt rotation and needs separate reset on both sides.
The Kerberos policy maximum ticket lifetime, which must be set to zero to purge forged tickets immediately after a reset.

quiz.explanation: Forged referral tickets signed with the inter-realm trust key are validated against that key, not against krbtgt, so rotating krbtgt does not invalidate them; the trust password must be reset on both sides in coordination with the partner. Two resets are the recommended practice because the prior password is retained for validation, and waiting for replication and ticket lifetime between them is what keeps replication healthy. Child domain krbtgt accounts also sign tickets, so every domain with KDC-level access needs rotation. Setting a ticket lifetime to zero is not a valid or useful remedy.

quiz.question: Which observation about trust discovery (T1482) is the best basis for escalating from low to medium severity?

options.label: A domain admin on a designated admin host lists the trusts during an approved change window for a new partner forest.
A monitoring service account reads trustedDomain objects every hour from a known management server, as it has done for months.
A sales workstation enumerates all trusts and foreign principals soon after a first-seen logon, then its user authenticates to the other forest.
A domain controller answers LDAP searches for trustedDomain objects from many clients as part of ordinary replication and referral work.

quiz.explanation: Discovery by itself is cheap, and any authenticated user can read trust objects, so the signal lies in context: an unexpected host and account, a recent first-seen logon, a broad sweep, and then authentication across a trust that the account has never used. The admin on an approved change window and the long-running monitoring account match the baseline and carry little concern. DCs responding to LDAP queries describe the server side of normal traffic and do not identify any suspicious client.

quiz.question: A security architect wants to limit what a lower-trust partner forest can do even if its identities are fully compromised. Which pairing of controls addresses both the claimed identities and the reachable resources?

options.label: Increase TGT lifetime and enable unconstrained delegation on trust-facing servers so tickets persist across the boundary.
Turn off auditing for logon events on trust-facing servers to reduce noise from foreign accounts and focus on local activity.
Add the partner's administrators to local administrator groups so that they can remediate issues in your forest themselves.
Keep SID filtering enabled so the partner cannot claim your SIDs, and use selective authentication so foreign users reach only explicitly allowed servers.

quiz.explanation: SID filtering restricts which identities the partner can assert, and selective authentication restricts which resources those identities may request through the Allowed to Authenticate permission; together with least-privilege grants they bound the damage of a compromised partner. Longer ticket life and unconstrained delegation enlarge the attacker's opportunities. Disabling logon auditing removes exactly the telemetry (4624, 4625, 4675) that exposes cross-trust abuse. Placing partner admins in local administrator groups hands a compromised forest direct privileged access, which is the opposite of containment.
